newsitem.title: GERMANY: German workers hit industry with protests.
newsitem.headline: German workers hit industry with protests.

text.p: Over 120,000 workers across Germany walked out on Tuesday to protest against major companies implementing a controversial new law aimed at cutting the cost to companies of sick-pay entitlements.

Worst hit was industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, which has spearheaded the attack on labour costs by adopting the law from the start of this month despite union protests that current sick payments are safeguarded in wage contracts.

Leaders of Daimler-Benz's work council estimated that 80,000 workers across more than 50 Daimler sites in Germany had walked out over the course of the day, with the figure expected to rise to 100,000 by the end of the Tuesday night shift.

Daimler's luxury car unit Mercedes Benz estimated that Tuesday's disruption, which included a walk-out by 10,000 workers at one if its main factories in the Stuttgart area had, with earlier stoppages, cost it alone some 220 million marks ($144.4 million) and 4,000 vehicles in lost production.

Worker representatives said Daimler and its management board, led by tough-talking chairman Juergen Schrempp, had made a serious misjudgement in thinking it could override existing wage pacts with the new law.

"Daimler Benz management obviously did not reckon with the reaction of the workforce," Daimler works council chairman Karl Feuerstein said after the demonstration in Stuttgart, adding that he had not seen such resistance by workers in 41 years at Mercedes.

The new law, approved as part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity plan aimed at whipping Germany's finances in shape for currency union, aims to trim 12 billion marks of wage costs which companies claim make them uncompetitive in world markets.
But workers say the 20 percent cut in sick pay envisaged by the new law would cost an employee on an average wage around 500 marks for a month of sickness.
Other major carmakers in Germany faced similar actions.
At Ford Motor Co's main factory in Cologne, about 12,000 workers stopped work during the early shift to attend a rally to press the company to explain what it intended to do on sick pay.
About 9,000 workers at other Ford plants owned by the U.S. carmaker were scheduled to hold demonstrations on Tuesday.

Another 7,000 workers at the Bochum plant of Adam Opel AG, a unit of U.S. car-maker General Motors Corp, also laid down their tools to attend a rally and protest at Opel's plans to implement the new law from the start of November.

But it is Daimler, which employs some 220,000 people across Germany, that has taken on the leading role in what Schrempp was quoted in a weekend report as calling the "fight for Germany as a place to do business."

Schrempp, who is also working on a large-scale management reorganisation at the group to make it more fleet-footed, is one of the fiercest advocates in the push by some German companies for higher profitibilty and thus greater shareholder value.

But Daimler was looking dangerously isolated on Tuesday as a number of other large companies said they were either continuing with the full sick pay entitlements or had agreed compromise measures with workers.

Carmaker Audi AG, a unit of Volkswagen AG, said its workers will receive 100 percent sick pay but that 20 percent of time lost will be put into "time accounts" in which workers will accrue "time debts" to be worked off or paid back.
Electronics giant Siemens AG also said it had agreed with its works council to continue making full wage payments to workers in the event of illness.

Chancellor Kohl has not made any specific comment on Daimler's quick implementation of the law but has said that companies should not break existing wage agreements to put it into effect -- something unions argue Daimler has done.
Workers representatives at the Stuttgart rally said they had now also received confirmation from Daimler that it planned to cancel existing agreements on Christmas and other bonus payments.
"We promise the Daimler board that this is only the beginning," Helmut Lense, chairman of the Mercedes works council at the Untertuerkheim plant in Stuttgart warned.
